title: SR&ED for Manufacturing Process Improvements | Canada FAQ
description: Canadian manufacturers can claim SR&ED for process improvements when the work is a systematic investigation seeking technological advancement.
summary: Canadian manufacturers can claim SR&ED incentives for process improvements when work is a systematic investigation seeking technological advancement to create new or improve existing processes, including incremental improvements. Commercial production and routine testing are excluded. Qualifying CCPCs earn a 35% refundable federal credit on up to $6,000,000 of qualified expenditures, and equipment acquired after December 15, 2024 is again eligible.

body.text: Canadian manufacturers can claim SR&ED incentives for process improvements when work is a systematic investigation seeking technological advancement to create new or improve existing processes, including incremental improvements. Commercial production and routine testing are excluded. Qualifying CCPCs earn a 35% refundable federal credit on up to $6,000,000 of qualified expenditures, and equipment acquired after December 15, 2024 is again eligible.
1. Executive and Legislative Architecture of the Canadian SR&ED Regime
1.1 Statutory Foundation and Macroeconomic Context

Canada's Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) tax incentive program represents the single largest federal source of financial support for business-led research and development, supporting more than 24,160 businesses annually across the country. Enacted in its modern dual-incentive structure in 1985, the program operates through two distinct yet interconnected statutory mechanisms codified within the federal Income Tax Act (ITA), R.S.C. 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.), and Part XXIX of the Income Tax Regulations (ITR), C.R.C., c. 945.

The first statutory pillar, governed by Section 37 of the ITA, establishes a dedicated pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures. This mechanism permits a taxpayer carrying on business in Canada to deduct 100% of allowable current—and, for property acquired after December 15, 2024, capital—SR&ED expenditures in calculating net income for the taxation year in which they are incurred, or to carry those pooled deductions forward indefinitely to offset taxable income in future taxation years. The second statutory pillar, governed by Sections 127 and 127.1 of the ITA, provides an Investment Tax Credit (ITC) ranging from a baseline rate of 15% to an enhanced rate of 35% on "qualified SR&ED expenditures," which may reduce federal Part I tax otherwise payable or yield a direct cash refund depending on the corporate classification and financial attributes of the claimant.

Despite the generosity of the SR&ED tax credit structure for early-stage enterprises, macroeconomic evaluations—including the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) 2025 Economic Survey of Canada—have consistently highlighted a structural paradox in which Canada's business-sector R&D investment intensity and per capita gross domestic product (GDP) productivity growth have lagged behind international peers. Historically, the sharp statutory phase-out of the 35% refundable credit at $10 million to $50 million of taxable capital, combined with the 2014 repeal of capital expenditure eligibility and the total exclusion of publicly listed domestic corporations from refundable credits, created a severe disincentive for mid-sized technology, manufacturing, and life sciences firms scaling within Canada. When domestic innovators executed an initial public offering (IPO) or acquired heavy compute and laboratory infrastructure, the abrupt loss of refundable SR&ED support altered their capital allocation calculus, frequently encouraging the migration of intellectual property and physical R&D assets to competing jurisdictions.
1.2 The 2024–2026 Legislative Overhaul and Enactment of Bill C-15

To rectify these structural impediments and modernize the statutory framework, the Department of Finance Canada initiated a two-phase legislative consultation process. Phase 1 ran from January 31, 2024 to April 15, 2024 to evaluate how the SR&ED program could better foster domestic productivity and intellectual property retention. Building upon stakeholder submissions from Phase 1, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance Chrystia Freeland tabled Budget 2024 on April 16, 2024, launching a second phase of technical consultations and committing an additional $600 million over four years, and $150 million per year ongoing, to enhance and modernize the SR&ED program.

Following the December 2024 Fall Economic Statement (FES 2024), the August 2025 release of draft legislative proposals by the Department of Finance, and the tabling of the 2025 Federal Budget on November 4, 2025, Parliament consolidated these reforms into Bill C-15, the Budget 2025 Implementation Act, No. 1 (S.C. 2026, c. 3). Bill C-15 received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026, enacting the most substantial expansion of the Canadian SR&ED regime in more than a decade.

The statutory amendments enacted under Bill C-15 fundamentally reshape corporate eligibility, expenditure caps, and asset qualification across four core dimensions. First, with respect to the enhanced expenditure limit, for taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024 (that is, after December 15, 2024), the maximum annual SR&ED expenditure limit eligible for the enhanced 35% ITC under subsection 127(10.2) of the ITA is doubled from $3,000,000 to $6,000,000, raising the maximum annual refundable ITC on current expenditures from $1,050,000 to $2,100,000. While initial December 2024 Fall Economic Statement proposals and August 2025 draft legislative commentary contemplated an intermediate $4.5 million limit, the final enacted provisions of Bill C-15 following Budget 2025 established the full $6.0 million ceiling.

Second, Bill C-15 significantly expands the phase-out thresholds and introduces an alternative revenue-based election. For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, the prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada phase-out range for Canadian-controlled private corporations (CCPCs) and their associated groups is increased from the former $10 million to $50 million corridor to $15 million to $75 million. Furthermore, CCPCs may now elect under subsections 127(10.31) or 127(10.32) of the ITA to have their expenditure limit phase-out determined using a three-year average gross revenue test ($15 million to $75 million) rather than taxable capital.

Third, the legislation extends the enhanced credit rate to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs). For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, amended subsections 127(9), 127(10.1), and 127(10.6) of the ITA grant ECPCs access to the enhanced 35% refundable ITC, phasing out their $6 million expenditure limit based on average gross revenue over the three preceding fiscal years between $15 million and $75 million.

Fourth, Bill C-15 restores eligibility for capital expenditures and shared-use equipment. By repealing paragraph 127(11.1)(c.1) and amending sections 37, 127, and 127.1 of the ITA, Parliament restored SR&ED deduction and ITC eligibility for new or used depreciable capital property acquired on or after December 16, 2024, as well as qualifying equipment lease costs that first become payable on or after December 16, 2024, alongside the reinstatement of Shared-Use Equipment (SUE) claims.
1.3 Summary Comparison of Pre- and Post-Bill C-15 Federal SR&ED Parameters

The transition between the legacy statutory rules and the post-Bill C-15 regime is governed strictly by the start date of the corporation's taxation year for rates, limits, and corporate status, and by the acquisition and available-for-use date of capital property for capital expenditures.

body.text: 2. Federal Investment Tax Credit Rates, Thresholds, and Corporate Eligibility
2.1 Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations and the Doubled Expenditure Limit

Under subsection 127(10.1) of the ITA, a corporation that is a Canadian-controlled private corporation (CCPC) throughout the taxation year is entitled to an additional 20% ITC on top of the baseline 15% ITC, yielding an aggregate 35% SR&ED ITC on qualified expenditures up to its annual expenditure limit. To maintain status as a CCPC as defined in subsection 125(7) and subsection 248(1) of the ITA, the corporation must be a private corporation that is a Canadian corporation and must not be controlled, directly or indirectly in any manner whatever (encompassing both de jure and de facto control under subsection 256(5.1)), by one or more non-resident persons, by one or more public corporations (other than a prescribed venture capital corporation), by a corporation with a class of shares listed on a designated stock exchange, or by any combination thereof. If a venture financing round results in non-resident investors or a public entity acquiring control, CCPC status is terminated for subsequent taxation years, restricting the corporation to the 15% non-refundable ITC unless it qualifies under the newly enacted ECPC rules.

For taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024, Bill C-15 doubled the baseline expenditure limit in subsection 127(10.2) from $3,000,000 to $6,000,000. Where a CCPC is associated (within the meaning of section 256 of the ITA) with one or more other CCPCs in a taxation year, the $6,000,000 expenditure limit must be shared among the associated group pursuant to subsection 127(10.21) and allocated via T2 Schedule 49 (Agreement Among Associated Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations to Allocate the Expenditure Limit). Furthermore, paragraph 87(2)(j.6) of the ITA enforces strict continuity upon corporate amalgamations, stipulating that the new corporation formed as a result of an amalgamation is deemed to be the same corporation as, and a continuation of, each predecessor corporation for purposes of calculating the expenditure limit under subsection 127(10.2).
2.2 Taxable Capital Phase-Out Mechanics and the Revenue-Based Election

Under amended subsection 127(10.2) of the ITA, a CCPC's $6,000,000 expenditure limit for a particular taxation year is reduced when its taxable capital employed in Canada (as determined under Part I.3 of the ITA, sections 181.2 to 181.4) for the immediately preceding taxation year—aggregated across all associated corporations—exceeds $15,000,000, and is eliminated entirely once prior-year taxable capital reaches $75,000,000.
Expressed mathematically for a standard 365-day taxation year, the expenditure limit under subsection 127(10.2) is calculated according to the statutory formula:
Within this statutory formula, the variable A is defined as:
A = min($60,000,000, max($0, Prior-Year Taxable Capital Employed in Canada − $15,000,000))

Under this linear reduction formula, every $1,000,000 of prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada above the $15,000,000 floor reduces the $6,000,000 expenditure limit by exactly $100,000. For instance, if a CCPC (or its associated group) recorded $35,000,000 of taxable capital employed in Canada in the preceding taxation year, its excess A under the post-Bill C-15 rules is $35,000,000 − $15,000,000 = $20,000,000 (compared to $35,000,000 − $10,000,000 = $25,000,000 under legacy rules). Its expenditure limit is therefore reduced by $2,000,000 to $4,000,000, yielding a maximum 35% ITC of $1,400,000 plus 15% on expenditures above the limit—providing a total ITC of $1,460,000 on a $4,400,000 claim, compared to only $393,750 at the enhanced rate under the legacy $3,000,000 and $10 million to $50 million formula.

A critical second-order compliance consequence arises from this amendment because the federal SR&ED taxable capital phase-out ($15,000,000 to $75,000,000) is now decoupled from the federal Small Business Deduction (SBD) taxable capital phase-out under subsection 125(5.1) of the ITA, which continues to grind the $500,000 active business limit between $10,000,000 and $50,000,000. Corporate tax planners can no longer rely on a single unified taxable capital calculation for both Schedule 23 (SBD allocation) and Schedule 49 (SR&ED expenditure limit allocation), and must verify both phase-out corridors independently for growing associated groups.

Even more significantly for capital-intensive innovators—such as clean-technology developers, biotechnology firms with substantial balance-sheet equity or debt, and advanced manufacturers—Bill C-15 introduced subsections 127(10.31) and 127(10.32) of the ITA. These provisions allow a CCPC (or an associated group of CCPCs) to elect out of the taxable capital grind under subsection 127(10.2) for a taxation year and instead compute its expenditure limit using the three-year average gross revenue phase-out ($15,000,000 to $75,000,000). Consequently, a pre-revenue or low-revenue biotechnology CCPC that has raised $80,000,000 in venture capital or convertible debt—which would otherwise push its taxable capital above $75,000,000 and reduce its enhanced SR&ED expenditure limit to nil—can file the election under subsection 127(10.31) and preserve the full $6,000,000 expenditure limit and $2,100,000 cash refund.
2.3 Expansion to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations

Historically, the moment a CCPC listed its shares on a designated stock exchange (such as the Toronto Stock Exchange or TSX Venture Exchange), it ceased to be a CCPC and immediately forfeited both the 35% enhanced ITC rate and any cash refundability, dropping to a 15% non-refundable credit. For taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024, Bill C-15 eliminates this "IPO penalty" by amending subsections 127(9), 127(10.1), 127(10.5), 127(10.6), and 127(10.61) of the ITA to extend the 35% enhanced refundable ITC to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs).

To qualify as an ECPC throughout a taxation year under subsection 127(9) of the ITA, a corporation must satisfy four cumulative statutory criteria, unless it qualifies as an "eligible subsidiary" under the same definition. First, the corporation must be resident in Canada throughout the taxation year. Second, it must be a public corporation, or be a corporation that would be a public corporation if the reference to a designated stock exchange in Canada were read as a reference to any designated stock exchange. Third, the corporation must not be controlled, directly or indirectly in any manner whatever, by one or more non-resident persons. Fourth, the corporation must not be one that would be controlled by any particular person if each share owned by a non-resident person were owned by that particular person.

Thus, while a foreign-listed multinational parent operating a Canadian subsidiary remains restricted to the 15% non-refundable ITC if controlled by non-residents, a domestic Canadian public company satisfies the ECPC definition. Under subsection 127(10.6) and consolidated group rules in subsection 127(10.61) (subject to application adjustments in subsection 127(10.64)), an ECPC's $6,000,000 expenditure limit is phased out on a straight-line basis when its average gross revenue over the three preceding fiscal years (computed from consolidated financial statements prepared in accordance with generally accepted accounting principles) is between $15,000,000 and $75,000,000, reaching nil at $75,000,000.
2.4 Refundability Architecture, Qualifying Corporations, and Carryforward Rules

Section 127.1 of the ITA governs the conversion of earned SR&ED ITCs into cash refunds. The statutory rate of refundability depends upon three variables: whether the expenditure is of a current or capital nature, whether the expenditure falls within or exceeds the corporation's annual expenditure limit, and whether the corporation meets the statutory definition of a "qualifying corporation" under subsection 127.1(2) or qualifies under subsection 127.1(2.01).

Under subsection 127.1(2) of the ITA, a "qualifying corporation" is a CCPC whose taxable income for the immediately preceding taxation year (aggregated with the taxable incomes of all associated corporations for their preceding taxation years) did not exceed its "qualifying income limit". For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, Bill C-15 expanded the qualifying income limit formula to align with the new $15,000,000 to $75,000,000 taxable capital range, increasing the denominator and cap from $40,000,000 to $60,000,000:

In this expression, A is nil if prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada is $15,000,000 or less, and otherwise equals the excess of prior-year taxable capital over $15,000,000, capped at $60,000,000.

Furthermore, subsection 127.1(2.01) of the ITA provides a vital statutory bridge for CCPCs that exceed their qualifying income limit (due to high prior-year taxable income) but remain within the taxable capital or elected revenue expenditure limit thresholds. For such a CCPC—provided it is not an "excluded corporation"—subsection 127.1(2.01) guarantees that the 35% ITC earned on SR&ED expenditures of a current nature within the expenditure limit remains 100% refundable. Status as a "qualifying corporation" under subsection 127.1(2) therefore matters primarily for determining whether the 15% ITC earned on expenditures exceeding the expenditure limit qualifies for a 40% refund.

body.text: Under subsections 127(5) and 127(9) of the ITA, any non-refundable ITC (or any refundable ITC that the taxpayer elects not to have refunded) may first be applied to reduce federal Part I tax payable for the current taxation year. Unused credits may be carried back up to 3 preceding taxation years (limited to the earlier year's Part I tax remaining after that year's credits) or carried forward up to 20 subsequent taxation years. Any ITC amount refunded in cash under section 127.1 is statutorily deemed to have been deducted from Part I tax payable, preventing double utilization through a subsequent carryback or carryforward.
2.5 Section 37 Deductible Pool and Paragraph 12(1)(t) Income Inclusion Mechanics

Allowable SR&ED expenditures incurred in Canada are accumulated in a dedicated expenditure pool under subsection 37(1) of the ITA. Unlike ordinary capital expenses subject to multi-year Capital Cost Allowance (CCA) depreciation schedules, the entire balance of the Section 37 SR&ED expenditure pool may be deducted in computing business income in the year incurred, or retained in the pool and carried forward indefinitely to shield future taxable profits.

However, the ITA prevents a double tax benefit on the same dollar of expenditure through a mandatory pool-reduction and income-inclusion mechanism operating across two sequential stages. First, with respect to government and non-government assistance, paragraph 37(1)(d) and subsection 127(9) of the ITA dictate that any government assistance (including provincial R&D tax credits and federal innovation grants) or non-government assistance that the taxpayer has received, is entitled to receive, or can reasonably be expected to receive in respect of SR&ED at the filing due date reduces both the Section 37 deductible expenditure pool and the qualified SR&ED expenditures eligible for the federal ITC in the current taxation year.

Second, with respect to the subsequent-year taxability of federal ITCs, paragraph 12(1)(t) and paragraph 37(1)(e) of the ITA stipulate that any federal SR&ED ITC claimed to offset Part I tax payable or received as a cash refund in a given taxation year reduces the Section 37 deductible SR&ED expenditure pool in the immediately following taxation year. To the extent that the prior year's federal ITC exceeds the remaining balance in the Section 37 pool—which routinely occurs when a taxpayer deducts its entire Section 37 pool each year—the negative pool balance is included directly in the corporation's taxable income in that following taxation year under paragraph 12(1)(t). Because the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) earns an ITC under Section 127 without ever entering the Section 37 deductible pool, the ITC attributable to the PPA inevitably triggers a paragraph 12(1)(t) income inclusion in the subsequent taxation year.
3. Technological Eligibility Criteria and Controlling Jurisprudence
3.1 Statutory Definition Under Subsection 248(1) of the ITA

The substantive legal gateway to the SR&ED program is the statutory definition of "scientific research and experimental development" in subsection 248(1) of the ITA. This definition conforms broadly to the international OECD Frascati Manual standards and requires a "systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis" across one of three primary categories. Under paragraph (a), eligible work encompasses basic research, defined as work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge without a specific practical application in view. Under paragraph (b), eligible work encompasses applied research, defined as work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge with a specific practical application in view. Under paragraph (c), which accounts for the vast majority of private-sector industrial and technology claims, eligible work encompasses experimental development, defined as work undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement for the purpose of creating new, or improving existing, materials, devices, products, or processes, including incremental improvements thereto.

Once a core project qualifies under paragraph (a), (b), or (c), paragraph (d) of the definition in subsection 248(1) extends eligibility to eight enumerated categories of support work—specifically engineering, design, operations research, mathematical analysis, computer programming, data collection, testing, or psychological research—provided that such work is commensurate with the needs, and directly in support, of the underlying basic research, applied research, or experimental development.

Conversely, paragraphs (e) through (k) of the definition in subsection 248(1) explicitly exclude specific commercial and routine activities from SR&ED qualification, even when performed by qualified scientists or engineers. Specifically, the statute excludes market research or sales promotion; quality control or routine testing of materials, devices, products, or processes; research in the social sciences or the humanities; prospecting, exploring, or drilling for, or producing, minerals, petroleum, or natural gas; the commercial production of a new or improved material, device, or product or the commercial use of a new or improved process; style changes; and routine data collection.
3.2 The Northwest Hydraulic Five-Question Common-Law Test

Because subsection 248(1) does not statutorily define terms such as "technological advancement," "systematic investigation," or "technological uncertainty," Canadian tax courts developed an authoritative common-law interpretive framework. In the landmark decision Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Ltd. v. The Queen, [1998] 3 C.T.C. 2520, 98 D.T.C. 1839 (T.C.C.), then Judge (later Chief Justice) Donald Bowman of the Tax Court of Canada articulated five cumulative questions that govern whether an activity constitutes SR&ED.

The first question asks whether there was a technological risk or uncertainty which could not be removed by routine engineering or standard procedures. Chief Justice Bowman emphasized that "routine engineering" encompasses all techniques, procedures, and data that are generally accessible to competent professionals in the field. If a problem can be resolved by applying established engineering principles or standard debugging, no technological uncertainty exists; however, if the resolution is not predictable on the basis of current state-of-the-art knowledge or experience—including "system uncertainty" arising from the integration of known technologies in a novel configuration—technological uncertainty is established.

The second question asks whether the person claiming to be doing SR&ED formulated hypotheses specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating that technological uncertainty. This entails a five-stage intellectual process: the observation of the subject matter of the problem, the formulation of a clear objective, the identification and articulation of the technological uncertainty, the formulation of a hypothesis or hypotheses designed to reduce or eliminate the uncertainty, and the methodical determination of a procedure to test the hypothesis.

The third question asks whether the procedures adopted accorded with the total discipline of the scientific method, including the formulation, testing, and modification of hypotheses. The court underscored that the methodology must be systematic and analytical from its inception, rather than intuitive trial-and-error tinkering.

The fourth question asks whether the process resulted in a technological advancement. A technological advancement represents an advancement in the general understanding of scientific or technological relationships—even a slight or incremental advancement, or the decisive rejection of a hypothesis that demonstrates a specific technological pathway is unviable under defined constraints. Crucially, commercial novelty or product functionality is distinct from technological advancement.

The fifth and final question asks whether a detailed record of the hypotheses tested and the results was kept as the work progressed. Particularly where the claimed advancements are incremental or occur within a commercial production environment, maintaining records generated contemporaneously with the experimental work is essential to corroborate that a systematic scientific investigation took place.
3.3 Administrative Guidelines Versus Binding Federal Court of Appeal Precedent

From its first publication in 2012 until 2021, the Canada Revenue Agency's administrative policy document—the Eligibility of Work for SR&ED Investment Tax Credits Policy—explicitly mirrored the five questions from Northwest Hydraulic. On August 13, 2021, however, the CRA archived that policy and published its revised Guidelines on the eligibility of work for SR&ED tax incentives. The 2021 CRA Guidelines reorganized the administrative review around two streamlined overarching inquiries known as the "Why" requirement and the "How" requirement. Under the "Why" requirement, the claimant must establish why the work is being conducted in order to advance scientific knowledge or for the purpose of achieving technological advancement. Under the "How" requirement, the claimant must demonstrate how the work is being conducted by means of a systematic investigation or search carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis. In the CRA's administrative breakdown, satisfying the "How" requirement entails demonstrating four operational elements: the generation of a hypothesis (an idea consistent with known facts serving as a starting point for investigation), the testing of that hypothesis by experiment or analysis, the development of logical conclusions based on experimental or analytical findings, and the keeping of evidence generated as the work progresses.

Following the 2021 administrative revision, taxpayers argued that the CRA's new two-step guideline had displaced or altered the legal threshold for SR&ED eligibility. The Federal Court of Appeal (FCA) had already reaffirmed the Northwest Hydraulic criteria in Kam-Press Metal Products Ltd. v. Canada, 2021 FCA 88 (May 10, 2021), aff'g 2019 TCC 246, rejecting the argument that the scientific-method criterion should not apply because that phrase does not appear in the statutory definition, and it addressed the revised guidance directly in National R&D Inc. v. Canada, 2022 FCA 72 (2022 CAF 72) (May 3, 2022), aff'g 2020 TCC 47, leave to appeal to S.C.C. refused, March 9, 2023 (No. 40303). In National R&D, the FCA held that the revised CRA guidance provides useful context but does not bind the courts, that its "How" requirement still reflects the need for rigour and discipline in the experimental process, and that the Tax Court did not err in applying the five-question framework established in Northwest Hydraulic, which remains the governing interpretation of the definition in subsection 248(1) of the ITA. Subsequent Tax Court of Canada decisions, including Manning Canning Kitchens Inc. v. His Majesty the King (analysed in late 2025 legal commentary), continue to adjudicate technical disputes strictly through the lens of Chief Justice Bowman's five questions.
4. Qualifying Expenditures and Calculation Frameworks
4.1 Salaries, Wages, and the 180-Day Unpaid Remuneration Rule

Salaries and wages typically represent the largest component of a Canadian SR&ED claim. Under subsections 37(1) and 37(8) of the ITA and subsection 2900(2) of the ITR, eligible remuneration consists of salaries or wages (as defined in subsection 248(1) as income from an office or employment under sections 5 to 8 of the ITA) paid to employees directly engaged in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada.

Whether an employee is "directly engaged" in SR&ED is determined strictly by the hands-on technical tasks performed—such as formulating hypotheses, designing experimental apparatus, writing experimental algorithms, executing test runs, or directly supervising technical personnel—rather than the employee's corporate title or academic credentials. Clerical, administrative, legal, human resources, and general executive management activities are not considered "directly engaged" hands-on work; they are instead categorized as overhead, which is captured either through the Prescribed Proxy Amount or, if incremental and directly related, under the Traditional Method.

Under limited statutory conditions (subsection 37(1.4), subsection 37(1.5) and lines 307 and 309 of Form T661), a claimant may also include permissible salary or wages for SR&ED performed outside Canada by Canadian-resident employees, capped at 10% of the total SR&ED salaries and wages paid to employees for SR&ED performed inside Canada during the taxation year.

A strict statutory timing rule governs accrued remuneration: pursuant to subsection 78(4) of the ITA, any salary, wages, or other remuneration accrued during the taxation year that remains unpaid on the day that is 180 days after the end of the taxation year is deemed not to have been incurred in that taxation year. On Form T661, such unpaid amounts must be reported on line 315 and excluded from the current year's SR&ED expenditure pool; they may only be claimed as an SR&ED expenditure in the subsequent taxation year in which they are actually paid, provided they are not a bonus or profit-based remuneration paid to a specified employee.
4.2 Specified Employees and Canada Pension Plan YMPE Ceilings

Special statutory anti-avoidance caps apply to "specified employees" to prevent owner-managers from artificially inflating refundable SR&ED tax credits (and the associated 55% proxy overhead calculation) by paying themselves large year-end salaries or bonuses. Under subsection 248(1) of the ITA, a "specified employee" of a person is an employee who either does not deal at arm's length with the employer (such as a spouse, child, or sibling of the controlling shareholder under section 251 of the ITA) or is a "specified shareholder" of the employer—meaning a person who owns, directly or indirectly at any time in the year, 10% or more of the issued shares of any class of the capital stock of the corporation or of any corporation related to the corporation.

For specified employees (reported on line 305 of Form T661 for work in Canada, and line 309 for permissible work outside Canada), three mandatory statutory restrictions apply. First, no portion of a bonus, commission, or remuneration based on profits paid to a specified employee is eligible as an SR&ED expenditure. Second, under paragraph 37(9.1)(b) of the ITA, the maximum amount of directly engaged salary or wages of a specified employee that can be included in the Section 37 SR&ED expenditure pool for a taxation year is limited to 5 times the Year's Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YMPE) determined under section 18 of the Canada Pension Plan (CPP) for the calendar year in which the taxation year ends, prorated by the number of days in the taxation year in which the individual is employed by the corporation and shared across associated corporations under subsections 37(9.2) through (9.5). Third, under subsections 2900(4) and 2900(7) of the ITR, the maximum amount of a specified employee's salary or wages that may be included in the salary base for computing the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) is restricted to the lesser of 75% of the specified employee's total salary or wages (for all duties, both SR&ED and non-SR&ED, excluding bonuses) from the employer in the year and 2.5 times the YMPE for the calendar year in which the taxation year ends, prorated for the number of days employed in the year.

Tax practitioners must note that while the federal government introduced a second earnings ceiling—the Year's Additional Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YAMPE) for second additional CPP contributions (CPP2) starting January 1, 2024 ($73,200 in 2024, $81,200 in 2025, and $85,000 in 2026 at a 4% contribution rate)—the statutory SR&ED formulas in the ITA and ITR remain anchored strictly to the first earnings ceiling (the YMPE).

body.text: 4.3 Overhead Calculation: Prescribed Proxy Method Versus Traditional Method

Under subsection 37(8) of the ITA and section 2900 of the ITR, a taxpayer must elect on Part 3 of Form T661 whether to compute SR&ED overhead using the Prescribed Proxy Method (line 160) or the Traditional Method (line 162). Once Form T661 is filed for a taxation year, the choice of method is irrevocable for that year.

Under the Prescribed Proxy Method, governed by subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B) of the ITA and subsection 2900(4) of the ITR, the taxpayer does not claim actual SR&ED overhead expenditures on Form T661. Instead, the taxpayer calculates a notional Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA)—reported on line 502 of Form T661—equal to 55% of the eligible SR&ED salary base, which comprises the directly engaged salaries of non-specified employees on lines 300 and 307 plus the capped salaries of specified employees on lines 305 and 309, less certain statutory exclusions. Note that the PPA rate has stood at 55% since 2014, having been reduced from the pre-2013 rate of 65%. Under subsections 2900(4) and 2900(6) through (9) of the ITR, the PPA is also subject to an overall cap linked to total business deductions net of specified exclusions such as building rent, CCA, and non-SR&ED outlays. As explained in Section 2.5, the PPA is included in "qualified SR&ED expenditures" in Part 4 of Form T661 to earn the 35% or 15% ITC, but is never added to the Section 37 deductible expenditure pool because the underlying actual overhead expenses are already deducted under ordinary business income rules.

Conversely, under the Traditional Method, governed by subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A) of the ITA and paragraph 2900(2)(c) and subsection 2900(3) of the ITR, the taxpayer foregoes the 55% PPA and instead itemizes actual overhead and other expenditures on line 360 of Form T661. To qualify under paragraph 2900(2)(c) and subsection 2900(3) of the ITR, each itemized overhead expenditure must be both directly related to the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada and incremental—meaning the expenditure would not have been incurred had the SR&ED not been carried out. Under the Traditional Method, eligible overhead includes employer portions of CPP, Employment Insurance (EI), and workers' compensation for directly engaged SR&ED staff, utilities consumed in dedicated R&D laboratories, travel directly required for SR&ED trials, and—following Bill C-15—lease costs incurred after December 15, 2024 for equipment used in SR&ED less than 90% of its operating time, prorated to actual SR&ED usage.

In practice, software, artificial intelligence, and engineering firms whose primary cost driver is technical payroll almost universally elect the Prescribed Proxy Method, as it delivers an automatic 55% uplift on eligible wages without requiring granular invoice-level substantiation of incremental overhead during a CRA financial audit. Conversely, heavy industrial, mining, or utility-intensive operations where incremental shop-floor consumables, specialized facility power, and partial-use equipment leases exceed 55% of direct technical wages may realize a larger claim under the Traditional Method.
4.4 Materials Consumed or Transformed and Commercial Production Runs

Under clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A) and subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(V) of the ITA and paragraph 2900(2)(a) of the ITR, a claimant under either the Proxy or Traditional Method may claim the cost of materials that are either consumed or transformed in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada. Materials consumed refer to physical supplies that are destroyed, rendered virtually valueless, or exhausted during experimental testing, such as chemical reagents, destructive test specimens, and laboratory gases. Materials transformed refer to materials that are physically integrated into an experimental prototype, pilot plant, or experimental production run that is subsequently sold or converted to commercial use, subject to the SR&ED Recapture Rules under subsections 127(27) to 127(35) of the ITA.

If a prototype, pilot plant, or batch of transformed materials whose cost was included in qualified SR&ED expenditures is subsequently sold or converted to commercial use within 10 taxation years of its acquisition, the lesser of the original qualified expenditure cost of the materials or property and the proceeds of disposition (or fair market value at the time of conversion to commercial use) triggers ITC Recapture on Schedule T2SCH31 (or Form T2038(IND)), adding the recaptured ITC directly back to Part I tax payable for that year.
4.5 Arm's-Length and Non-Arm's-Length Subcontractors and Third-Party Payments

Canadian SR&ED legislation distinguishes sharply between arm's-length and non-arm's-length contracting arrangements, as well as third-party payments to approved research entities. Where a claimant enters into an arm's-length SR&ED contract with a Canadian resident (corporation or individual) to perform SR&ED or eligible paragraph 248(1)(d) support work on the claimant's behalf in Canada, 100% of the contract expenditure is deductible in the Section 37 pool. However, for purposes of calculating "qualified SR&ED expenditures" in Part 4 of Form T661 to earn the Section 127 ITC, only 80% of the arm's-length contract payment is eligible—reflecting a mandatory 20% statutory reduction under subsection 127(9) designed to strip out the contractor's assumed commercial profit margin.

Where a claimant enters into a non-arm's-length SR&ED contract (such as with a parent, subsidiary, or sister corporation) to perform SR&ED on its behalf, the contract payment is not automatically a qualified expenditure for ITC purposes. Instead, the non-arm's-length performer incurs the underlying SR&ED expenditures and may transfer the qualified expenditures (up to the contract amount, net of capital or assistance adjustments) to the payer by jointly executing Form T1146 (Agreement to Transfer Qualified Expenditures Incurred in Respect of SR&ED Contracts Between Persons Not Dealing at Arm's Length), reported on lines 508 and 510 by the transferee and lines 540, 544, and 546 by the transferor on Form T661. Similarly, Form T1145 governs the allocation of SR&ED assistance between non-arm's-length parties. Finally, third-party payments under subparagraphs 37(1)(a)(ii) and (iii) made to an approved university, college, research institute, or non-profit SR&ED corporation in Canada for SR&ED carried on in Canada related to the taxpayer's business (where the taxpayer is entitled to exploit the results) are subject to the same 80% inclusion rule for ITC calculation and are reported on Part 3, line 370 of Form T661.
4.6 Restoration of Capital Expenditures, Lease Costs, and Shared-Use Equipment

Between January 1, 2014 and December 15, 2024, all capital expenditures (and related capital lease costs) were statutorily barred from both the Section 37 SR&ED deduction pool and the Section 127 ITC calculation under former paragraph 37(1)(b) and former paragraph 127(11.1)(c.1). Under Bill C-15 (enacted March 26, 2026), Parliament repealed paragraph 127(11.1)(c.1) and amended sections 37, 127, and 127.1 to fully restore SR&ED capital expenditures for new or used depreciable property acquired on or after December 16, 2024, and for equipment lease costs that first become payable on or after December 16, 2024. This legislative restoration represents a major financial windfall for hardware-intensive sectors, including artificial intelligence and machine learning companies acquiring high-performance GPU clusters and compute servers, biotechnology and pharmaceutical laboratories, clean-energy pilot facilities, and modular construction innovators.

To claim restored SR&ED capital expenditures on line 390 (and project-level lines 262 and 263) or Shared-Use Equipment on line 504 of updated Form T661 (Version 26), a taxpayer must navigate five strict statutory and administrative rules. First, the asset must satisfy the All-or-Substantially-All (ASA — 90%) Intent Test. To qualify as a 100% SR&ED capital expenditure on line 390 of Form T661, the expenditure must be made to acquire new or used depreciable property (excluding buildings, leasehold interests in buildings, land, inventory, or goodwill) that the taxpayer intended, at the time of acquisition, either to use all or substantially all (defined by the CRA as 90% or more) of the operating time in its expected useful life to perform SR&ED in Canada, or to consume all or substantially all (90% or more) of its value in performing SR&ED in Canada. Capital cost includes the purchase price, installation costs, customs and excise duties, transportation, and directly attributable acquisition costs. If the corporation's taxation year began before December 16, 2024 (straddling the effective date), SR&ED operating time percentage must be calculated over the total operating time for the period after December 15, 2024.

Second, capital claims are governed by the Available-for-Use Timing Rule under subsection 37(1.2) (for the Section 37 deduction) and subsection 127(11.2) (for the Section 127 ITC) of the ITA. Under these provisions, an SR&ED capital expenditure is deemed not to have been made until the depreciable property is considered to have become available for use by the taxpayer—meaning delivered, assembled, and capable of performing its intended function in the SR&ED project. This statutory rule creates both a compliance trap and a transitional planning opportunity. From a compliance perspective, specialized laboratory or compute equipment ordered and paid for in late December 2026 that is not delivered and commissioned until February 2027 cannot be claimed on the 2026 Form T661, and instead slides into the 2027 taxation year. Conversely, as highlighted in specialized tax analysis examining amended subsection 127(11.2), equipment purchased prior to December 16, 2024 that only became available for use on or after December 16, 2024 may be deemed acquired on the available-for-use date for ITC purposes under subsection 127(11.2).

Third, where a manufacturer or technology firm acquires new depreciable equipment (other than general-purpose office equipment or furniture, GPOEF) that is used primarily (more than 50%, but less than 90%) of its operating time for SR&ED in Canada and the remainder for commercial production, Bill C-15 restored the Shared-Use Equipment (SUE) mechanism on line 504 of Form T661. Under the First-Term SUE rule, if the new equipment is used primarily (greater than 50% of operating time) for SR&ED in Canada during its first period of operating time (a minimum of 12 months, ending at the end of the first taxation year that finishes at least 12 months after acquisition), the claimant may include 25% of the capital cost of the equipment in qualified expenditures. Under the Second-Term SUE rule, if the equipment continues to be used primarily (greater than 50% of operating time) for SR&ED in Canada through the second period (ending at the end of the first taxation year that finishes at least 24 months after acquisition), the claimant may include an additional 25% of the capital cost, bringing total inclusion to 50% of capital cost across both periods.

Fourth, Bill C-15 restores eligibility for equipment lease costs that first become payable after December 15, 2024. Under both the Proxy and Traditional Methods, lease costs incurred after December 15, 2024 for depreciable equipment (excluding GPOEF under the Proxy Method) used 90% or more (ASA) of its operating time in SR&ED qualify in full (or at 50% if leased equipment is used primarily, between 50% and 90%, under the Proxy Method SUE rules). Furthermore, under the Traditional Method, lease costs incurred after December 15, 2024 for equipment used in SR&ED less than 90% of the time may be claimed on line 360 as overhead and other expenditures to the extent incremental and directly related.

Fifth, where capital assets acquired for R&D or digital operations do not satisfy the SR&ED 90% ASA or >50% SUE tests—for example, a server cluster that also hosts a commercial production environment—Bill C-15 provides a powerful parallel tax incentive under the Capital Cost Allowance (CCA) system. Specifically, Bill C-15 enacts 100% immediate expensing for qualifying property acquired on or after April 16, 2024 and available for use before January 1, 2027 in Class 44 (patents or rights to use patented information), Class 46 (data network infrastructure equipment and related systems software), and Class 50 (general-purpose electronic data-processing equipment and systems software), alongside the temporary reinstatement of the Accelerated Investment Incentive (AII) for eligible property acquired after 2024 and available for use before 2030.
5. Administrative Governance, 2026 Tax Forms, and Statutory Filing Deadlines
5.1 Dual Institutional Governance: Department of Finance and Canada Revenue Agency

The administration of the Canadian SR&ED regime is divided between two federal institutions with distinct statutory mandates. The Department of Finance Canada retains sole responsibility for drafting tax legislation, setting statutory credit rates and expenditure limits, conducting macroeconomic policy consultations, and negotiating tax harmonization agreements with the provinces. Conversely, the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) administers and enforces the SR&ED program nationwide through its specialized SR&ED Directorate and regional Tax Services Offices. Within the CRA, SR&ED claims are evaluated through a bifurcated review model in which Research and Technology Advisors (RTAs)—who hold degrees and industry experience in engineering, computer science, or natural sciences—assess whether the claimed projects satisfy the technological eligibility criteria under subsection 248(1) of the ITA, while Financial Reviewers (FRs)—who are accounting and tax audit specialists—verify the mathematical accuracy, payment proof, specified employee caps, overhead elections, and capital expenditure compliance under sections 37, 127, and 127.1.
5.2 Granular Architecture of Updated Form T661 (Version 26) and Associated Schedules

Following the Royal Assent of Bill C-15 on March 26, 2026, the CRA released a comprehensive suite of updated SR&ED tax forms in May 2026 to operationalize the new $6,000,000 expenditure limit, ECPC eligibility, and capital expenditure lines. On May 15, 2026, the CRA published Form T661 (Version 26), Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Expenditures Claim (accompanied by interim CRA line-by-line filing instructions while Guide T4088 undergoes revision), alongside Form T1145 (Agreement to Allocate Assistance for SR&ED Between Persons Not Dealing at Arm's Length) and Form T1146 (Agreement to Transfer Qualified Expenditures Incurred in Respect of SR&ED Contracts Between Persons Not Dealing at Arm's Length). On May 22, 2026, the CRA published updated T2 Schedule 31 (T2SCH31), Investment Tax Credit – Corporations (used by corporations to calculate the 35% and 15% ITCs, ECPC revenue phase-outs, CCPC revenue elections, ITC carrybacks and carryforwards, and ITC recapture, while individuals use Form T2038(IND)). On May 29, 2026, the CRA published updated T2 Schedule 49 (T2SCH49), Agreement Among Associated Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations to Allocate the Expenditure Limit.
Form T661 (Version 26) is structured into 10 mandatory parts, with specific line numbers governing both technical project narratives and financial calculations:

body.text: For partnerships, the CRA's administrative and statutory rules dictate that the partnership itself must file a single Form T661 reporting 100% of the partnership's SR&ED expenditures (deducted in computing the partnership's net income at the partnership level), while allocating the resulting ITC to eligible members via T5013 slips; individual partners cannot add partnership SR&ED costs to their own separate Section 37 pools.
5.3 The Strict 18-Month Statutory Reporting Deadline and Pre-Claim Approval

Under subsection 37(11) and paragraphs 127(9)(m) and (m.1) of the ITA, a taxpayer's SR&ED reporting deadline is 12 months after the taxpayer's income tax return filing due date for the taxation year in which the expenditures were incurred. Because a corporation's T2 return filing due date under paragraph 150(1)(a) of the ITA is 6 months after the end of its taxation year, a corporation's absolute statutory deadline to file a complete Form T661 and Schedule T2SCH31 is 18 months after the end of its taxation year. For example, for a corporation with a December 31, 2024 taxation year-end, the T2 was due June 30, 2025, and the absolute SR&ED reporting deadline was June 30, 2026. For a corporation with a December 31, 2026 taxation year-end, the T2 is due June 30, 2027, and the absolute SR&ED reporting deadline is June 30, 2028. By contrast, an individual carrying on an unincorporated business has a T1 filing due date of June 15 of the following calendar year, yielding an SR&ED reporting deadline of 17.5 months after the December 31 taxation year-end (June 15 of the second following year), whereas a trust's T3 return is due 90 days after year-end, yielding a 15-month SR&ED reporting deadline.

The 18-month corporate filing deadline is a strict statutory bar ("statute-barred" upon expiry). If a corporation fails to file the prescribed forms containing the prescribed information (specifically project descriptions in Part 2, expenditure line items in Parts 3 and 4, and Schedule 31) on or before the 18-month mark, the expenditure is permanently disqualified from both the Section 37 SR&ED pool and the Section 127 ITC, and the Minister of National Revenue has no discretionary authority under the Taxpayer Relief Provisions (subsection 220(3.1) of the ITA) to waive or extend the deadline.

To provide up-front certainty prior to filing, the CRA administers an optional Pre-Claim Approval program. Under this framework, a business may apply to the CRA to have its project's technical eligibility assessed before commencing work or incurring expenditures. A corporation may submit up to 3 projects for Pre-Claim Approval, with each approval remaining valid for up to 3 taxation years (reported on new lines 212 and 214 of Form T661 Version 26), though the corporation must still file its standard annual T661 and Schedule 31 to substantiate actual costs incurred. Furthermore, in conjunction with the enactment of Bill C-15 in March 2026, the CRA implemented administrative processing reforms designed to cut average SR&ED claim processing times by approximately 50%.
5.4 CRA Technical and Financial Review Protocols and Contemporaneous Evidence

When an SR&ED claim is selected for a technical and financial review by the CRA, the burden of proof rests entirely upon the taxpayer to substantiate both technological eligibility and financial accuracy using contemporaneous documentation—records generated naturally at the time the experimental work was performed, rather than reconstructed a posteriori during claim preparation.

During a combined RTA and FR review, auditors examine two primary evidentiary streams. With respect to technical evidence supporting Part 2 of Form T661, CRA Research and Technology Advisors inspect design specifications, source-code version control commits (such as Git repositories with technical commit messages), issue-tracking tickets documenting failed experimental iterations, bench test logs, laboratory notebooks, simulation outputs, mathematical models, and internal technical post-mortems demonstrating the progression from hypothesis formulation to logical conclusion. With respect to financial evidence supporting Parts 3 through 6 of Form T661, CRA Financial Reviewers audit contemporaneous time-tracking sheets or project allocation logs linking each employee's hours to specific SR&ED projects (essential where engineers split their time between SR&ED and commercial development, such as 60% SR&ED versus 40% routine maintenance), T4 payroll summaries, general ledger sub-accounts, proof of payment within 180 days of year-end, arm's-length contractor statements of work and invoices explicitly referencing SR&ED tasks performed in Canada, and asset usage logs proving that post-December 15, 2024 capital equipment met the ≥ 90% ASA or > 50% SUE operating-time thresholds.
6. Provincial and Territorial R&D Tax Regimes and Inter-Jurisdictional Stacking

Every Canadian province (except Prince Edward Island, which delivers R&D support solely through direct innovation grants rather than a statutory corporate income tax credit) and the Yukon Territory operates a dedicated R&D tax incentive program that piggybacks on—or runs parallel to—the federal SR&ED definition. Between 2025 and 2026, provincial legislatures enacted transformative structural reforms, led by Quebec's complete replacement of its legacy R&D credits with the new CRIC regime and British Columbia, Ontario, Saskatchewan, Manitoba, and the Atlantic provinces harmonizing with federal Bill C-15.
6.1 Quebec: The 2025–2026 CRIC Consolidation and Elimination of Legacy Credits

In its 2025–2026 Budget (detailed in Revenu Québec's official Tax News bulletin published on July 9, 2025), the Government of Quebec executed the most comprehensive overhaul of provincial R&D taxation in Canada. Effective for taxation years or fiscal periods beginning after March 25, 2025, Quebec abolished seven legacy tax measures: the tax credit for salaries and wages of researchers (the traditional R&D salary tax credit, formerly Form RD-1029.7); the tax credit for university research or research carried out by a public research centre or a research consortium; the tax credit for fees and dues paid to a research consortium; the tax credit for private partnership pre-competitive research; the tax credit for technological adaptation services; the industrial design component of the design tax credits (retaining only the fashion design component); and the personal income tax holiday for foreign researchers and experts.

In place of these fragmented credits, Quebec enacted the unified Tax Credit for R&D, Innovation and Pre-Commercialization (CRIC — Crédit d'impôt pour la R-D, l'innovation et la précommercialisation), administered by Revenu Québec and claimed on Form RD-1029.8.CR-T (2026-09 version), accompanied by Form RD-1029.8.EN-T (Agreement Regarding the Expenditure Limit for the Tax Credit for R&D and Pre-Commercialization) and Form RD-1029.8.PR-T (Information Regarding the Pre-Commercialization Component).

The architecture of the new Quebec CRIC regime encompasses four defining structural features. First, the CRIC is 100% refundable for all qualified corporations (regardless of taxable capital or public or private status) at an enhanced rate of 30% on the first $1,000,000 of eligible R&D and pre-commercialization expenditures in excess of the exclusion threshold (shared among associated corporations via Form RD-1029.8.EN-T), and 20% on eligible expenditures exceeding the $1,000,000 limit. Second, unlike the federal SR&ED program—which terminates once technological uncertainty is resolved—the CRIC explicitly extends eligibility to pre-commercialization expenditures, including regulatory certification, homologation, product validation tests, and industrial design or commercial prototyping activities aimed at bringing an R&D innovation to market. Third, aligning with federal Bill C-15, the CRIC makes capital expenditures relating to the acquisition of depreciable property used in R&D and pre-commercialization in Quebec eligible for the tax credit, reported on line 61a of the Quebec corporate return for taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025. Fourth, to refocus tax assistance on higher-value-added jobs, each qualified corporation or partnership is subject to an annual exclusion threshold equal to the greater of $50,000 or the sum of the R&D employees threshold and the pre-commercialization employees threshold. The per-employee annual exclusion cap (prorated by time devoted to R&D or pre-commercialization) is set at $75,000 for a taxation year or fiscal period ending on or before March 18, 2026, and increases to $85,000 for a taxation year beginning after March 18, 2026.
6.2 Ontario: OITC, ORDTC, and Harmonized Capital Expenditure Restoration

Ontario administers two complementary corporate R&D tax credits under the Taxation Act, 2007 (Ontario), both filed alongside the federal T2 return and administered by the CRA. The first program, the Ontario Innovation Tax Credit (OITC — T2 Schedule 566), provides an 8% fully refundable tax credit to qualifying corporations (CCPCs with a permanent establishment in Ontario) on up to $3,000,000 of qualified Ontario SR&ED expenditures per taxation year, yielding up to $240,000 in cash refunds. The $3,000,000 OITC expenditure limit phases out when prior-year federal taxable income is between $500,000 and $800,000 or when the prior-year specified capital amount is between $25,000,000 and $50,000,000. The second program, the Ontario Research and Development Tax Credit (ORDTC — T2 Schedule 508 and Worksheet S580WS), provides a 3.5% non-refundable tax credit to all corporations (including large public and foreign-controlled corporations, as well as CCPCs on expenditures net of the OITC) with no expenditure cap, carrying back 3 years and forward 20 years. Because the 8% OITC constitutes government assistance, any OITC claimed (unless formally waived) reduces the qualified expenditure pool eligible for the 3.5% ORDTC.

Because Ontario's statutory definitions of qualified expenditures in the Taxation Act, 2007 cross-reference section 127 of the federal ITA, the Royal Assent of federal Bill C-15 on March 26, 2026 automatically restored capital expenditure eligibility for both the 8% OITC (Schedule 566) and the 3.5% ORDTC (Schedule 508) for depreciable property acquired on or after December 16, 2024. As confirmed in the annex to Ontario's 2026 Fall Economic Statement, this restoration is projected to provide more than $50 million in additional tax relief over three years to approximately 700 Ontario businesses, notwithstanding that the general informational webpage on ontario.ca had not yet caught up as of October 30, 2026 and still displayed the legacy 2013 capital exclusion notice. Capital property acquired between January 1, 2014 and December 15, 2024 remains excluded from both Ontario credits.
6.3 British Columbia: Bill 2 Enhancements, ECPC Access, and Permanent Extension

British Columbia provides the British Columbia Scientific Research and Experimental Development Tax Credit (BCRDTC) under Part 6 of the Income Tax Act (British Columbia), claimed on T2 Schedule 425 (Form T666). The BCRDTC provides a 10% refundable tax credit up to the expenditure limit for qualifying corporations, and a 10% non-refundable tax credit for expenditures above the limit or for non-qualifying corporations, with a 3-year carryback and 10-year carryforward.

On April 16, 2026, British Columbia's Bill 2 received Royal Assent, enacting four major enhancements to harmonize Schedule 425 with federal Bill C-15. First, for taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024, the BC refundable expenditure limit is doubled from $3,000,000 to $6,000,000 (raising the maximum annual refundable BC credit from $300,000 to $600,000), phasing out in lockstep with the federal taxable capital and revenue thresholds ($15 million to $75 million). Second, Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) can now claim the 10% refundable BC SR&ED tax credit on up to $6,000,000 of BC qualified expenditures. Third, depreciable capital property acquired after December 15, 2024 (alongside Shared-Use Equipment) is once again included in BC qualified expenditures, calculated via the new Capital column in Schedule A of Schedule 425 and reported on line 350. Fourth, the statutory sunset clause—which had previously been extended from September 1, 2022 to September 1, 2027—has been permanently repealed, making the BCRDTC a permanent feature of British Columbia's corporate tax structure.
6.4 Alberta: Innovation Employment Grant Baseline and Incremental Mechanics

Effective for taxation years beginning on or after January 1, 2021, Alberta replaced its former 10% R&D tax credit with the Alberta Innovation Employment Grant (IEG), administered separately by Alberta Treasury Board and Finance (Tax and Revenue Administration) via the Alberta Corporate Income Tax Return on AT1 Schedule 29 (Alberta Innovation Employment Grant) and AT1 Schedule 29 Listing (Listing of Innovation Employment Grant Projects Carried out in Alberta), pursuant to Information Circular IEG-1.

The Alberta IEG is a 100% refundable grant delivered through the corporate tax system to corporations (both CCPCs and non-CCPCs, provided they satisfy the taxable capital threshold) with a permanent establishment in Alberta that incur qualified SR&ED expenditures (as defined federally, including post-December 15, 2024 capital expenditures) in Alberta. The program operates through a two-tier incremental rate structure: corporations earn an 8% refundable base grant on all eligible Alberta SR&ED expenditures up to the corporation's "base amount" (calculated as the average of the corporation's qualified Alberta SR&ED expenditures over the two immediately preceding taxation years), plus an additional 12% incremental bonus grant—bringing the combined rate to 20% refundable—on eligible Alberta SR&ED expenditures that exceed the two-year rolling base amount. For a newly formed startup with zero SR&ED spending in the prior two years, its base amount is nil, meaning 100% of its first-year eligible Alberta SR&ED spending earns the full 20% refundable grant. The maximum annual eligible expenditure limit is $4,000,000 (shared among associated corporations on AT1 Schedule 29, yielding a maximum annual refundable grant of $800,000 at the 20% incremental rate). Unlike the federal Bill C-15 expansion to $15 million–$75 million, the Alberta IEG continues to phase out on a sliding scale when prior-year federal taxable capital employed in Canada is between $10,000,000 and $50,000,000, becoming nil at $50,000,000.
6.5 Saskatchewan, Manitoba, Atlantic Canada, and Yukon Regimes

All remaining provincial and territorial R&D tax credit schedules were updated in 2026 to incorporate the federal Bill C-15 restoration of capital expenditures and shared-use equipment. In Saskatchewan, the Saskatchewan Research and Development Tax Credit (T2 Schedule 403) provides a 10% tax credit on eligible SR&ED expenditures incurred in the province. Following post-Bill C-15 updates to Schedule 403 (Part 4), for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, the annual expenditure limit eligible for the 10% refundable credit for CCPCs doubled from $1,000,000 to $2,000,000, yielding up to $200,000 in refundable cash entered on line 645 of Schedule 5. Eligible expenditures exceeding the $2,000,000 refundable limit, as well as expenditures incurred by non-CCPCs, earn a 10% non-refundable credit (entered on line 631 of Schedule 5, with a 10-year carryforward and 3-year carryback), subject to an aggregate combined annual credit ceiling of $1,000,000 ($10,000,000 of expenditures).

In Manitoba, the Manitoba Research and Development Tax Credit (T2 Schedule 380), governed by sections 7.3 and 7.4 of the Income Tax Act (Manitoba), provides a 15% tax credit to all corporations incurring eligible SR&ED expenditures in Manitoba. Where R&D is performed in-house, 50% of the credit is refundable (an effective 7.5% cash refund, entered on line 613 of Schedule 5) and 50% is non-refundable (an effective 7.5% non-refundable credit, entered on line 606 of Schedule 5, with a 20-year carryforward and 3-year carryback). Where R&D is conducted under an eligible contract with a qualifying post-secondary or research institute, 100% of the 15% credit is refundable. Corporations may renounce the non-refundable portion under subsection 7.3(7) of the Manitoba Act to avoid grinding their federal SR&ED pool.

Across Atlantic Canada and the North, Nova Scotia (Nova Scotia Research and Development Tax Credit — T2 Schedule 340), New Brunswick (New Brunswick Research and Development Tax Credit — T2 Schedule 360), and Newfoundland and Labrador (Newfoundland and Labrador Research and Development Tax Credit — T2 Schedule 301) each provide a 15% fully refundable tax credit to all corporations regardless of size or CCPC status with no expenditure cap, updated for post-December 15, 2024 capital expenditures. On Nova Scotia's Schedule 340, which must be filed no later than 18 months after the corporation's tax year-end, the credit is reported on line 566 of Schedule 5 and any property recapture is reported on line 221 of Schedule 5. Finally, Yukon (Yukon Research and Development Tax Credit — T2 Schedule 442) provides a 15% fully refundable tax credit on eligible SR&ED expenditures incurred in Yukon by any corporation or individual, plus an additional 5% refundable bonus credit (20% total) on payments made to Yukon University.
6.6 Comprehensive Provincial and Territorial R&D Tax Incentive Matrix

body.text: 6.7 Federal-Provincial Assistance Grinding and Net Effective Tax Benefit Modelling

Because provincial R&D tax credits (as well as direct innovation grants such as NRC-IRAP) are statutorily classified as "government assistance" under subsection 127(9) and paragraph 37(1)(d) of the ITA, they cannot simply be added linearly to the 35% federal ITC. Instead, provincial credits earned in the year reduce the federal qualified SR&ED expenditure base dollar-for-dollar before the 35% (or 15%) federal ITC rate is applied. Crucially, however, most provinces—including British Columbia, Alberta, Saskatchewan, Manitoba, and the Atlantic provinces—compute their provincial R&D credit on the expenditure base including the federal Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA), whereas Ontario's OITC reduces the ORDTC base, and Quebec's CRIC computes its credit directly on eligible R&D and pre-commercialization salaries, contracts, and capital above the exclusion threshold without applying the federal 55% PPA.

To illustrate the exact statutory mechanics under the enacted 2026 rules, consider a qualifying CCPC (with prior-year taxable capital under $15,000,000, thus entitled to the full $6,000,000 federal expenditure limit) that elects the Prescribed Proxy Method (55% PPA) and incurs $1,000,000 of directly engaged non-specified employee SR&ED salaries in calendar year 2026. Adding the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount ($550,000) to the $1,000,000 direct salary outlay yields a Gross Federal Qualified Expenditure Base (Pre-Assistance) of $1,550,000.

In British Columbia (10% Refundable BCRDTC on Schedule 425), the corporation earns a 10% BC credit on the $1,550,000 qualified expenditure base equal to $155,000 in cash. Deducting that $155,000 of provincial government assistance leaves a net federal qualified expenditure base of $1,395,000, which generates a 35% federal SR&ED ITC of $488,250 in cash—yielding a combined immediate cash refund of $643,250, or 64.33% of the $1,000,000 direct salary outlay.

In Ontario (8% Refundable OITC on Schedule 566 plus 3.5% Non-Refundable ORDTC on Schedule 508), the corporation first earns an 8% OITC on $1,550,000 equal to $124,000 in cash. The OITC reduces the eligible base for the 3.5% ORDTC to $1,426,000, generating $49,910 in non-refundable ORDTC. Both Ontario credits reduce the federal qualified expenditure base to $1,376,090, which generates a 35% federal cash refund of $481,631.50—yielding $605,631.50 in immediate cash refunds (60.56% of direct salary) plus $49,910 in non-refundable ORDTC, for a total combined credit value of $655,541.50 (65.55% of direct salary). If the Ontario startup is in a multi-year tax loss position and cannot utilize the non-refundable 3.5% ORDTC, formally waiving the ORDTC preserves $49,910 in the federal base, increasing the immediate 35% federal cash refund by $17,468.50 to $499,100 (for total immediate cash of $623,100, or 62.31% of direct salary).

In Nova Scotia and Atlantic Canada (15% Refundable Credit on Schedules 340, 360, or 301), the corporation earns a 15% provincial refundable credit on $1,550,000 equal to $232,500 in cash. Deducting that $232,500 leaves a net federal qualified expenditure base of $1,317,500, which generates a 35% federal cash refund of $461,125—yielding a combined immediate cash refund of $693,625, or 69.36% of the $1,000,000 direct salary outlay.

body.text: 7. Strategic Tax Planning and Compliance Conclusions

The enactment of Bill C-15 on March 26, 2026, alongside Quebec's 2025–2026 CRIC consolidation and British Columbia's Bill 2 (April 16, 2026), fundamentally transforms the compliance and strategic planning landscape for Canadian R&D claimants across four operational areas.

First, corporate claimants and their tax advisors must conduct an immediate retroactive review of 2025 taxation years. Because the doubled $6,000,000 expenditure limit, the $15,000,000 to $75,000,000 taxable capital phase-out, the CCPC gross-revenue election, and ECPC eligibility apply to all taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024 (including calendar-year 2025 claims), any CCPC or ECPC that filed its 2025 T2 return under the legacy $3,000,000 limit or excluded capital property acquired on or after December 16, 2024 should file an amended Form T661 (Version 26) and Schedule T2SCH31 prior to its 18-month statutory reporting deadline.

Second, election modelling for capital-heavy CCPCs is now a mandatory annual compliance step. Venture-backed CCPCs in biotechnology, hardware, and clean technology with balance-sheet taxable capital exceeding $15,000,000—but whose three-year average gross revenue remains below $15,000,000—must proactively execute the new election under subsection 127(10.31) or 127(10.32) of the ITA on Schedule 31 to substitute the revenue-based test for the taxable capital grind, thereby preserving up to $2,100,000 in annual federal refundable credits.

Third, engineering and finance teams must establish rigorous capital asset metering and available-for-use governance. With capital expenditures and Shared-Use Equipment restored for depreciable property acquired after December 15, 2024, claimants must maintain contemporaneous operating-time metering logs from the date of commissioning to substantiate either the ≥ 90% ASA threshold (Line 390) or the > 50% SUE threshold (Line 504), while ensuring that hardware deliveries are commissioned into active R&D service before year-end to satisfy the subsection 37(1.2) and 127(11.2) available-for-use rules.

Fourth, tax directors should systematically evaluate waiving or renouncing non-refundable provincial credits when in a non-taxable position. In jurisdictions with non-refundable provincial R&D credits—specifically Ontario's 3.5% ORDTC on Schedule 508 and the 50% non-refundable half of Manitoba's credit on Schedule 380—loss-making CCPCs can optimize immediate liquidity by waiving or renouncing the non-refundable provincial credit so that it does not grind the 35% fully refundable federal ITC base.
